## The penalized fit {#sec-statmod-inner}

With the hyperparameters held, what is minimized is the negative
log-likelihood plus the penalties the terms declare:

$$
\mathcal{O}(\beta; \vartheta) \;=\; -\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \,
\log f\!\left(y_i; \theta_i(\beta)\right) \;+\; \sum_{k} \rho_k(\beta; \vartheta_k) .
$$

Neither part is averaged. A penalty is a negative log-prior, as
@sec-penalty-definition sets it out, and a posterior adds a log-likelihood
and a log-prior at full size; dividing one of them by $n$ would leave
$\vartheta$ meaning something that depends on the sample size, so that the
same prior scale would describe different beliefs at $n = 10^2$ and at
$n = 10^5$. What is scaled instead is the rule that stops the loop. The fit
of a single distribution in @sec-fitting divides the objective by $n$ and
compares an unscaled threshold against it; here the objective is left alone
and the threshold reads a quantity that carries no sample size, and in both
places the thing being arranged is that a tolerance mean the same at
$n = 10$ and at $n = 10^7$.

### Two kinds of block {#sec-statmod-split}

The terms divide by a property each of them already reports. A penalty whose
kink set, in the sense of @sec-penalty-branches, is empty is twice
differentiable in the coefficients, so its block has a curvature and can
enter a system solved with one. Everything of that kind goes into a single
system and is estimated all at once: an unpenalized block, a ridge, a spline,
a random effect, a structured or additive penalty. Their joint curvature
exists, and using it is what closes a fit in a handful of iterations.

A penalty with a kink -- a lasso, a SCAD, an MCP -- has no second derivative
at the point its own mode sits on, and its block is estimated by a method of
its own with everything else held fixed, through the proximal operator of
@sec-penalty-branches. The fit alternates between the two until the objective
and every block stop moving.

The split is a question put to the penalty and not a list of term names, so a
term whose penalty is replaced by a smooth approximation moves into the first
group with nothing here to change.

### The scoring step {#sec-statmod-scoring}

Write $\Omega_i$ for the $K \times K$ information of observation $i$ with
respect to its own $K$ predictors, multiplied by that observation's weight,
and $Z$ for the design that stacks the equations' blocks. The step solves

$$
\left(Z' \Omega Z + S(\vartheta)\right) \delta \;=\; Z'g - S(\vartheta)\beta ,
$$

with $g$ the score with respect to the predictors and $S$ the penalties'
Hessian. Taking $\Omega_i$ to be the expected information makes this Fisher
scoring, and the blocks are then positive definite wherever the family is
regular, so a step is usable from a poor starting point. Taking the observed
Hessian makes it Newton, which converges faster near the optimum and is the
curvature an exact gradient of the marginal criterion is written against.

The two matrices are never assembled. Each $\Omega_i$ has a Cholesky factor
$L_i L_i' = \Omega_i$, computed by writing the recursion out over the $K$
indices and evaluating each entry over all $n$ observations at once, so no
loop runs over the sample; stacking those factors against the design gives
$R$ with $R'R = Z'\Omega Z$. The penalty has a factor $C$ with $C'C = S$,
taken from an eigendecomposition with the non-positive directions dropped,
which is what a penalty of deficient rank requires: a spline's is deficient
by exactly the dimension of its null space, and a Cholesky has nothing to
return there. The step is then a decomposition of

$$
A \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} R \\ C \end{bmatrix}, \qquad A'A \;=\; Z'\Omega Z + S ,
$$

and neither cross-product is formed. A design whose condition number is
$\kappa$ is decomposed at $\kappa$, where forming the normal equations would
present the decomposition with $\kappa^2$. That matters most where the design
is worst conditioned by construction: the working design of a break-point
term is bounded only to $\epsilon^{-1/2}$, so squaring it exhausts double
precision.

A diagonal penalty is factored by taking the square root of its diagonal,
which is the same answer the eigendecomposition gives, the eigenvalues of a
diagonal matrix being its diagonal entries. The case is worth detecting for
how often it arises: a ridge is diagonal, a random effect is diagonal, and
the Demmler-Reinsch penalty of @sec-terms-catalog is
$\operatorname{diag}(0, 1, \ldots, 1)$ exactly, as is any block-diagonal
assembly of them.

Where the objective is quadratic in $\beta$ the whole loop is one solve, and
the answer is available in closed form to compare against. Holding the scale
of a Gaussian family fixed does exactly that:

```{r}
#| label: closed-ridge
set.seed(20260828)
n_ridge <- 80
d_ridge <- data.frame(x = runif(n_ridge, -2, 2))
d_ridge$R <- matrix(rnorm(n_ridge * 3), n_ridge, 3)
d_ridge$y <- 1 + 0.8 * d_ridge$x +
  as.numeric(d_ridge$R %*% c(0.6, -0.4, 0)) + rnorm(n_ridge, sd = 0.7)

lam <- 2.5
ridge_fit <- statmod(y ~ x + ridge(R, lambda = lam),
                     fixed(gaussian1_distrib(), sigma = 1), d_ridge)

Zr <- cbind(1, d_ridge$x, d_ridge$R)
Sr <- diag(c(0, 0, rep(lam, 3)))
closed <- as.numeric(solve(crossprod(Zr) + Sr, crossprod(Zr, d_ridge$y)))

cbind(fitted = unname(coef(ridge_fit)$mu), closed = closed)
```

The ridge's hyperparameter is a precision, so it enters that solve as it
stands rather than as one over a square, and the intercept and the slope are
unpenalized, which is why the penalty matrix carries two zeros.

### The rank of the augmented matrix {#sec-statmod-rank}

A decomposition has to say whether the matrix it was handed is of full rank,
and the test reads the diagonal of the triangular factor divided by each
column's norm. Since $A'A = R'R$, scaling the columns of $A$ scales that
diagonal by the same factors, so the ratio is the diagonal of a decomposition
whose columns have unit norm.

Reading the raw diagonal instead reports a matrix as near-singular whenever
its columns differ in size, which is what a large smoothing parameter does to
the penalty rows of its own block standing beside an unpenalized one. Those
matrices are not near-singular; per-column scaling forgives a separation of
scale from any source, while an exact collinearity stays exactly singular
under it. The distinction is worth a measurement: on a model with a random
intercept, the raw test rejected 87 of 127 solves that the dense route finds
at full rank, and the equilibrated ratio over the same solves stayed between
0.445 and 1.

Sparsity survives the whole construction. A grouping indicator has density
$1/m$ over $m$ groups, the square-root design built from it is sparse, and the
augmented matrix is decomposed by a sparse QR, which is a QR and keeps the
conditioning property the augmented form was chosen for. A sparse Cholesky of
the normal equations would be faster still and would give that property up.

### Blocks that move with their coefficients {#sec-statmod-moving}

A design block is usually a function of the data alone. The nonlinear term
and the break-point terms of @sec-terms-catalog are not: their block is the
Jacobian of the contribution at the current coefficients, so it moves as the
fit moves. Writing $f(\beta)$ for what such a term contributes and $X(\beta)$
for its block, the difference

$$
\mathrm{adj} \;=\; f(\beta) - X(\beta)\,\beta
$$

is added to the predictor as a per-observation adjustment. Every
cross-product in the step then reads the block as it stands, and the
increment the step returns is the Gauss-Newton one for that term. The
arrangement covers both constructions with no branch. For a continuous
break-point the adjustment is not zero and the iteration is Gauss-Newton; for
a discontinuous one the columns satisfy $X\beta = f$ exactly, by the identity
that writes an indicator as $\tfrac12 + (x - \psi)/(2\lvert x - \psi\rvert)$,
so the adjustment vanishes and the same step is the working fit of
@fasola2018.

Such a block is refreshed once per sweep rather than once per trial point. A
discontinuous term's rescaling factor halves whenever its break-point
reverses direction, which is a fact about the path and not about the point:
refreshing it inside a line search would advance that schedule at every trial
the search rejects, and refreshing it from the specification would freeze it
at its starting value and solve a permanently smoothed problem instead.

### When the loop stops {#sec-statmod-stop}

The rule that drives the loop compares the score per observation,
$\max_j \lvert g_j \rvert / n$, against a tolerance, so that the threshold
means the same at $n = 10$ and at $n = 10^7$. Any criterion object of
@sec-optimizers7 may drive it instead, and since the state's gradient is that
same per-observation score, `crit_grad(t)` is exactly the tolerance $t$.

The verdict a fit reports is arbitrated by a second reading, dimensionless in
the response's units. Writing $\mathcal{J}_p$ for the coordinates equation
$p$ owns and $H$ for the information's diagonal, it is

$$
\max_{j \in \mathcal{J}_p} \frac{\lvert g_j \rvert}{n\, s_p},
\qquad s_p = \sqrt{\operatorname{median}_{j \in \mathcal{J}_p} H_{jj} / n} ,
$$

read per equation and maximized over them. The score of a location equation
carries the units $1/y$ and its curvature $1/y^2$, so the ratio survives any
rescaling of the response, which the absolute rule alone does not. This
reading can relabel a run that stalled at the optimum as converged and can
never stop one that is still moving; driving the loop with it was tried and
fails at large $y$, where the guard on a stalled objective fires before a
rule $1/s_p$ stricter can.

A term whose block is a frozen working linearization answers the question for
itself. The gradient the layer computes there belongs to the working model,
and the profile objective of a discontinuous break-point term is a step
function in the position with no gradient to vanish, so what ends that fit is
the term's own report that its construction has reached a fixed point.
